t.chennai@13.1,80.3:
Chennai was Madras until 1996, and it is a place where tradition and technology sit side by side. The city grew up around Fort St George, which the East India Company began building in 1644, and the fort still stands near the seafront, now home to the state government. A short distance south, in the old quarter of Mylapore, the Kapaleeshwarar Temple rises in a colourful tower of carved gods and animals, and the streets around it are lined with shops selling jasmine, brass lamps and sweets.

With more than four million people, the city is the capital of Tamil Nadu and a centre of music, dance and film. The Marina, a long beach along the seafront, is crowded each evening with families, vendors and kite-flyers. Filter coffee, idli and dosa, served on banana leaves, are the staples of breakfast, and a plate of rice and sambar at a small restaurant is a satisfying meal for very little money.

The ride to Mahabalipuram follows the East Coast Road, one of the most pleasant roads in southern India. It leaves the city through the suburbs, then runs along the coast for about fifty kilometres, with the sea on one side and backwaters, salt pans and casuarina groves on the other. Fuel is easy in the city and along the road, and the surface is mostly good, though traffic can be heavy at weekends, with buses and cars heading for the beaches. Early morning is best, when the air is cool and the light is clear.

The climate is hot and humid, with the northeast monsoon from October to December bringing heavy rain, and the best riding months are January to March. Take water, a hat and plenty of patience for the city streets. By the time the road opens out along the sea, you will have forgotten the traffic.
t.mukunda nayanar temple@12.6,80.2:
Mahabalipuram, the Seven Pagodas of old sailors' charts, was a port city of the Pallava kings, who ruled this coast from their capital at Kanchipuram in the seventh and eighth centuries. Their sculptors worked in granite, carving temples out of the living rock and building others from cut stone, and the town is now full of the results. The Mukunda Nayanar Temple is one of the smaller and quieter of them, a modest stone shrine of the eighth century dedicated to Shiva, standing a little apart from the crowds in the north-west of the old town.

It is not a showpiece, and that is its charm. You can walk around it in a few minutes, look at the weathered stonework and the plain doorway, and have it almost to yourself on a weekday morning. The point of stopping is the context: here is the same hand that made the great monuments by the sea, working in a smaller, simpler key. Nearby lie fields, palms and small houses, and the sound of chisels tapping carries from the stone-carvers' workshops that line the streets, where sculptors still make gods and animals for temples around the world.

Mahabalipuram has about 12,000 people, and it is small enough that fuel and food are easy to find, with a few stations along the main road and many cafés near the shore temple. The East Coast Road gets you here from Chennai in a couple of hours. Be careful with speed bumps at villages, and with the traffic of buses and cars on weekends. Park near the main complex, where guards keep watch, and walk.

The sea is never far. In the evening a breeze comes off the Bay of Bengal, the heat softens, and the carved stone turns the colour of honey. It is the best time to wander, when the day trippers have gone, and to sit with a glass of lime soda and think about how long these granite shapes have been standing here in the salt wind.
t.pidari ratha valian kuttai ratha@12.6,80:
Cut from a single boulder, the Pidari Ratha and its neighbour the Valayankuttai Ratha belong to the earliest generation of monuments at Mahabalipuram. The Pallava sculptors who made them in the seventh century worked from the top down, starting at the roof and carving inwards and downwards through the rock, a method that left no room for mistakes. The result is a small, compact temple form, square and neat, with a pyramidal roof, and some of the details were never finished, so you can still see where the chisels stopped.

The word ratha means chariot, though these are not vehicles but shrines, and the name was given later, when local people noticed a resemblance to the processional carts used in temple festivals. They stand on the northern side of the site, among scattered rocks and sandy ground, a short walk from the main group, and the area has a quiet and slightly abandoned feel, with goats grazing in the shade and children playing nearby.

The town of Mahabalipuram, with about 12,000 people, is close, and a handful of cafés and small shops serve visitors. Fuel stations stand on the main road, and the East Coast Road from Chennai brings you here in about two hours. Parking is easy near the ticket office, and guards will watch the bike. The site is open daily during daylight hours, and entry is charged, with lower prices for locals.

Come early. By late morning the sun is fierce, the granite is hot to touch, and the sandy paths reflect a glare that is hard on the eyes. In the soft light just after sunrise, the carved shapes cast long shadows and the sea breeze carries the smell of salt and woodsmoke. It is a good moment to look closely at the stone, to see the marks of the tools, and to marvel at the confidence of sculptors who started with a rough rock and ended with a temple.
t.main complex of mahabalipuram@12.6,80.2:
The main complex at Mahabalipuram is a stone anthology of Pallava art, set between a low granite hill and the Bay of Bengal. Its centrepiece is the Shore Temple, built in the early eighth century under King Rajasimha, a pair of slim, tapering towers of weathered granite that stand almost at the water's edge. Sea winds have rounded the carvings, and in the morning light the temple looks like a sandcastle that has been left to harden for thirteen centuries. It survived the tsunami of 2004, when the sea drew back and exposed more ancient structures on the sand.

Not far inland, a huge rock face carries the relief known as Arjuna's Penance, or the Descent of the Ganges, a panel some twenty metres long crowded with gods, elephants, monkeys, hunters and ascetics, all carved with astonishing liveliness. Nearby, a vast round boulder called Krishna's Butter Ball rests on a slope as though it were about to roll away, though it has stayed in place for ages, and local children slide down the rock beside it. The five Rathas, carved from single blocks and named after the Pandava brothers of the Mahabharata, form another highlight.

The site is a UNESCO World Heritage listing, with entry charged and set opening hours. The town of Mahabalipuram, with about 12,000 people, wraps around it, and has guesthouses, cafés and seafood restaurants, as well as shops selling stone carvings. Fuel is available on the main road, but not in the old streets. Traffic and parking are manageable, though weekends bring crowds from Chennai, who arrive in buses and cars.

The best time is early morning or late afternoon, when the light is warm and the heat is bearable. In the cooler months, from November to February, the sea breeze is kind. Wander slowly, as the monuments are scattered, and take a break in the shade. The carvings reward patience, and the Shore Temple, seen from the beach at sunset, stays in the memory.
t.salvador@-13.0,-38.5:
Salvador is the oldest city in Brazil in the sense that matters, because it was the first capital, founded by the Portuguese in 1549 and ruling the colony until 1763. It sits on a peninsula at the mouth of the Baía de Todos os Santos, a big bay with islands, and its old centre, the Pelourinho, is a hillside of colourful colonial houses, baroque churches and cobbled streets, listed by UNESCO in 1985. The name Pelourinho means pillory, which tells you something about what once happened in the square.

This is also the heart of Afro-Brazilian culture. Salvador received more enslaved Africans than any other port in the Americas, and their descendants shaped the city's music, religion and food. Candomblé temples hold ceremonies on the hills, capoeira circles form in the squares, and drummers fill the old streets with rhythm. On every corner a woman in white lace sells acarajé, a fritter of black-eyed peas fried in palm oil and filled with shrimp and spicy paste, a dish with roots in West Africa that you really must try. Carnival here is louder, longer and more street-based than anywhere else in Brazil.

As a place to ride, Salvador is exciting rather than relaxing. Traffic is heavy and fast, with motorcycle couriers weaving between lanes and buses that stop without warning, and the steep streets of the old town have slippery cobbles and sharp gradients. Do not leave anything on the bike, and park it in a guarded lot if you can. The Lacerda Elevator carries people between the lower city and the upper one, and the ferry to Itaparica Island is a pleasant way to leave the traffic behind.

The Chapada Diamantina loop starts by heading inland on the BR-324, which crosses a hot plain of farmland and scrub before climbing to the highlands, and the distances are long, so fill up before leaving the city. Fuel is plentiful in Salvador, but less so in smaller towns.

The sunsets from the Barra lighthouse are famous, and the crowds who gather there to applaud the sun are part of the show.
t.kapalua@21.0,-156.7:
Kapalua is a low-key resort on the north-west tip of Maui, built on what was once a huge pineapple plantation, and it sits on a coast of bays, headlands and lava rock facing the island of Molokai across the channel. The plantation land is now golf courses and condominiums, with some pineapple fields still hanging on, but the setting is lovely, with the green West Maui Mountains rising behind and the sea bright blue in front. Honolua Bay, just along the coast, is a marine reserve known for snorkelling in summer and big surf in winter.

Near here, the road heads into one of the most dramatic and demanding rides on the island. The Kahekili Highway wraps around the rugged north coast of West Maui, past blowholes, sea cliffs and tiny villages, and it is narrow and winding, with long stretches of single lane, blind corners and steep drops. It is named for Kahekili, the Maui chief who ruled much of the islands in the eighteenth century. Many rental car agreements prohibit driving it, because of the risk, and the road demands your full concentration, with slow speeds and frequent use of the horn on blind turns.

The scenery is spectacular, with deep green valleys, waterfalls after rain, and a cliffside road dropping to sea level and back up again. Nakalele Point has a blowhole that sends water spurting skyward when the swell is up, and a rough trail leads to a lighthouse, but the lava rock is sharp and dangerous in heavy surf. The sea here is powerful, and people have been swept off the rocks. Wet weather is also a hazard, making the road greasy and prone to rockfall, so avoid it in heavy rain.

Practical matters need care. Lahaina, the old whaling capital and royal seat, was devastated by a wildfire in August 2023, and the community is still recovering, so be respectful and patient if you pass through. Carry water and food, and keep a good distance on blind curves. Mornings are best, when there is less traffic, and the light is clear.
t.nakalele blowhole@21.0,-156.6:
Maui's northwest coast looks at first like a place designed to scare people, and Nakalele is where that begins to make sense. The Kahekili Highway wraps around a rocky headland with the surf pounding the black lava below, and a short, rough walk across the rocks leads down to the blowhole, a hole in the lava shelf through which waves shoot a jet of water high into the air. In big surf the spout can rise many metres, with a roar and a boom that you feel in your chest. It is spectacular and genuinely dangerous: people have been swept off the rocks here, and the signs warning you to stay back are not suggestions.

The road itself is the real adventure. The Kahekili Highway, Route 340, is named for the last independent king of Maui, who ruled in the eighteenth century, and it is a narrow, twisting road with blind corners, a single lane in places and long drops to the ocean. It is paved, but the surface is patchy, and the width demands patience. Many rental companies forbid it, so check your contract. On a motorcycle it is a slow, rewarding ride, about as far from a highway as the word allows. Mornings are best, before the traffic of tour vans builds up, and heavy rain can cause rockfalls and closures.

The land here is dry and windswept, a surprise in a place usually thought of as lush. Lava shelves, sea cliffs and low scrub run to the water, and the colours are rust, black and blue. Nakalele Point has a lighthouse, and the coastline nearby has a place called the Dragon's Teeth, a jagged lava formation. Hawaiian history is everywhere, with old fishing shrines and house platforms scattered across the headlands, which should not be disturbed.

There are no services here, and little shade. The nearest sizeable towns are Napili-Honokowai and Lahaina on the west side, where you can fill up and eat, and Wailuku on the other. Take on petrol before starting the road, because the next station may be a long way off. Bring water, sturdy shoes, and respect for the surf. If the waves look big, watch from a distance. The sunsets here, with the island of Molokai across the channel, are good.
t.kahakuloa@21.0,-156.5:
Kahakuloa is a village that most people drive past in a minute and remember for years. It sits in a steep green valley on Maui's northwest coast, where the Kahekili Highway dips from the cliffs to a small bay, with a church and a handful of houses, taro patches along the stream, and a great domed headland, Kahakuloa Head, standing guard at the seaward end. The headland rises more than 600 feet from the water and is a famous landmark, a volcanic plug that glows a rich green in the morning sun.

This is one of the few places on Maui where traditional life has held on. Families have lived here for generations, growing taro and fishing, and the little church, with its white steeple and blue roof, is a photographer's favourite. The village is small and private, and visitors are asked to be respectful: keep your voice down, do not wander into yards, and park where the signs say. Roadside stands sell banana bread and fruit, which is worth buying if you find a stand open.

The road is the challenge. North of Kahakuloa the highway narrows to a single lane in places, with blind curves, steep drops and the occasional pothole, and the surface can be broken by rain. The route between here and Honolua Bay is slow and rough, so do not plan to hurry. The southern approach, from Wailuku, is a little easier, but still twisty, with a series of hairpins as it climbs and descends between valleys. Mornings are the best time, when the light is soft and traffic is light.

Wailuku, about twelve kilometres away, and the neighbouring towns of Waihee have petrol stations, and Lahaina and Kapalua on the west side have more. Take food and water, since the stands are sporadic. Weather can switch from sun to rain in a minute, and wet tarmac under overhanging foliage demands care. Check that your hire agreement allows the road. Leave the village as you found it, and drive carefully on the way out, because the next bend is always tighter than the last.
t.wailuku@20.9,-156.5:
Wailuku is the county seat of Maui and one of the oldest towns on the island, a modest place of about fifteen thousand people on the slopes below the West Maui Mountains, where the valley of ʻĪao opens onto the central isthmus. It is often overlooked by visitors rushing between the airport and the beaches, which is a pity, because the town has an unpretentious charm, with historic buildings, small restaurants, antique shops and a slower rhythm than the resorts.

The valley behind the town is a place of deep significance. ʻĪao Valley State Monument is a steep, green gorge with a slender volcanic spire, the ʻĪao Needle, rising from the forest, and its stream runs clear and cold. In 1790, the Battle of Kepaniwai took place here, when Kamehameha the Great's forces defeated the army of Maui, and legend says the stream was choked with bodies. Today the valley is peaceful, with rainforest, mist and birdsong. It is also one of the wettest places on the island, so bring a jacket.

For a rider, Wailuku is the end of the Kahekili Highway, after a long, slow, twisting ride around the north coast, and the first sight of a proper town, with traffic lights and supermarkets, can come as a relief. The roads here are wide and busy, and the contrast with the winding coastal road is sharp. Kahului, a larger town only a few kilometres away, has the main harbour, airport and shopping centres, and Wailuku and Kahului together form the commercial heart of the island.

You will find fuel and food on the main roads, and the town has a number of small restaurants serving local dishes: saimin noodle soup, plate lunches, and fresh poke, as well as fresh baked goods. The old Bailey House museum, a former mission building, has a collection of Hawaiian artefacts and paintings. Weather in the town is usually dry and warm, though the valley often catches showers, and the trade winds keep the air fresh. Early morning is a quiet time, and a short walk in the old streets makes a good ending to the day.
t.kahului@20.9,-156.5:
Kahului is where most people land on Maui, and for a rider it is the last flat, tidy, six-lane stretch of the day. The town sits on the isthmus between the two volcanoes, with Haleakalā's enormous grey-green shoulder rising to the south and the older, jagged West Maui Mountains to the west. It is a planned town, laid out by the sugar company in the middle of the last century to house plantation workers, which is why it feels more like a grid of shopping centres and bungalows than a postcard. That is fine. You are here for the practical things.

Do them properly before you leave. Kahului has proper fuel, more than you will see again until you are back, and a big wholesale store near the airport is known for cheap petrol. Eat something real, because the Hana Highway has food stands and banana bread but not much in the way of a sit-down lunch, and fill your water bottle. Wailuku, the old county seat, is a few minutes along and has the better old-fashioned coffee shops if you want to do the morning properly.

The ride begins by heading east on Hana Highway through sugarcane country that is mostly fallow now; the last big mill at Puʻunēnē closed in 2016, and the fields have been going to grass and new crops since. After Pāʻia, a former plantation town that turned into a surf-and-sunscreen stop, the road narrows, the trade-wind rain forest closes in, and the numbering starts to matter. Locals count mile markers rather than corners, and the famous tally of hundreds of curves and dozens of one-lane bridges is not exaggerated. Start early.

A word on weather. Kahului itself is dry and breezy, and the leeward side can be bright and hot while the windward coast is soaked, so pack a rain layer even when the airport is blazing. If it has rained for days, landslides and flooded stream crossings are possible on the far side, so check conditions with a local before committing. Otherwise, this is a rare place where the best part of the trip begins ten minutes from baggage claim.

The north shore beyond Pāʻia has some of the best wind and waves in the Pacific, and you will pass the cliff lookout at Hoʻokipa where windsurfers and turtles share the water. Keep that in mind when you are tempted to hurry through the first few miles: the opening is half the show.
t.paia@20.9,-156.4:
Paia is where the Hana Highway properly starts, even though the road has been climbing out of the Kahului plain for some time already. It is an old sugar and plantation town on Maui's north shore, a short row of weathered wooden storefronts, surf shops, and cafes with a very relaxed idea of the clock. Windsurfers and kitesurfers gather at the beaches nearby, and the trade winds that make them happy are the same ones that keep the air here cool and slightly salty.

Treat Paia as the last easy stop before the long haul. Haiku-Pauwela, a few kilometres on, and Makawao up the slope are bigger places, but this is where most riders settle their breakfast and their petrol. The road beyond is a slow business: it is often said to have well over six hundred bends and dozens of narrow bridges, many of them single lane, and the real total matters less than the rhythm. You are never going to get a run on it. Tour vans, rental cars, and drivers who have stopped dead for a waterfall will set the pace, and the sensible approach is to accept that and enjoy the jungle instead.

The town's history is the history of Hawaii's sugar era in miniature. Plantation workers came from Japan, Portugal, the Philippines, and China to cut cane for the mills, and you can still feel their mix in the old temples, the bakeries, and the faces on the street. The mill chimney is gone from the skyline, and the trade now is tourists and surfers, but the little wooden town keeps its plantation scale. It is a fine place to learn how a very international island came to be.

Come early. By nine the street fills and parking becomes a negotiation, and a rider who wants Hana before the afternoon showers should be rolling by eight. Ride it on a weekday if you can. Showers can arrive from the mountain at any hour, so a rain layer on the bike is no weakness. Bring cash for the roadside stalls farther along, and top up the tank here or just down the hill, because stations get scarce once you are into the rainforest.
t.keanae@20.9,-156.1:
Halfway along the Hana Highway the land does something unexpected: it flattens. A black lava peninsula pushes out into the Pacific, and on it sits Keanae, a Hawaiian village of taro patches, a small stone church, and a shoreline where the surf throws itself at dark rock with real violence. After miles of tunnelled jungle and blind hairpins, the sudden view of open sea and green fields is a small shock.

The peninsula was formed when late lava flows from Haleakala ran down the volcano's flank to the coast. The soil here is rich and the water plentiful, which is why the village has grown kalo, or taro, in flooded terraces for a very long time. Taro is the staple of traditional Hawaiian life, pounded into poi, and the neat patches visible from the road are one of the few places on Maui where you can see the old farming still in use. The church, built of lava stone mortared with coral, dates from the nineteenth century and is a simple, sturdy thing that has faced a great deal of weather.

The road to the peninsula is a short detour off the main highway, narrow and quiet, and worth the few minutes. There is a roadside stand near the junction with a reputation for banana bread, and you will likely see a line of people for it, which is often a good sign in a place with so few shops.

The ocean here is not for swimming. The rocks are sharp, the currents strong, and waves can surge higher than they look. Stand back from the edge and take photographs from the church lawn or the lookout. The light is best in the morning, when the sun clears the mountain behind you and the taro leaves are bright. Rain moves through quickly in this part of Maui, and the road stays slick under the trees. Take it carefully, and give the bridges the respect they deserve.
t.hana@20.8,-156.0:
There is a particular kind of satisfaction in arriving at Hana, which has little to do with the town itself. Hana is small, a post office and a scattering of houses, a bay, a few shops, and the sense that the world has been politely asked to stay outside. You come here because the ride was long and the road gave you no choice. A little over fifty miles, ridden at the honest pace the highway demands, takes a good part of a morning, and the pleasure is in having done it.

The surroundings are a quiet kind of dramatic: pastureland sloping up to the flanks of Haleakala, the sea on the other side, and old lava rock walls in between. Hana has long been a ranching and farming community, and before the road was built it was reached mostly by boat. Its isolation has shaped it. People here talk about the place with a kind of protective fondness, and a rider who behaves like a guest will be treated like one. Hana Bay has a black sand beach and a small park, good for a quiet half hour with a sandwich bought somewhere on the way.

Fuel is the question to settle before the ride, not after. The town does have a small station, but it keeps short hours and is not something to rely on. The reliable plan is to fill the tank in Paia or Kahului and keep a margin for the way back, which is the same distance on the same road. Food is simple: a general store, a few lunch stands, and a couple of cafes that can run out of things by mid-afternoon. Bring cash and patience.

From here, the road continues south around the volcano, past Kipahulu, where Charles Lindbergh is buried in a small churchyard by the sea. The surface changes to patched and sometimes rough, with long, exposed stretches that open into a very different, dry landscape on the far side. Plenty of riders turn back at Hana, and that is perfectly respectable. If you do, leave by early afternoon so that the descent through the rainforest happens in daylight and the tour vans are in front of you rather than behind.
t.wailua falls@20.7,-156.0:
The advantage of Wailua Falls is that you do not have to earn it. A few miles past Hana, beyond the point where many visitors turn around, the road crosses a bridge, and the waterfall appears beside it: a clean drop of roughly eighty feet into a green pool, fed by a stream that never seems to run dry. There is a pull-off, a short path, and usually a small crowd with cameras. After hours of focusing on bends and bridges, it makes a welcome and easy reward.

The setting is lush even by Maui standards. This side of Haleakala catches the full force of the trade wind rain, and the slopes above the road hold dense forest of guava, hau, and fern. The water that comes over the lip has fallen on the mountain, collected in streams, and arrives here after a short, steep run. The volcanic rock under it was laid down in successive flows, and the stair-step shape of the falls shows how the stream has cut through layers of different hardness over time.

Wailua Falls is on the road toward Kipahulu and the Haleakala national park coast, and beyond it the road is a mixed bag. Stretches are narrow, and the surface can be broken, with one-lane sections where you simply have to read the corner and give way. The local drivers know it well and are not in a hurry. Do not expect fuel anywhere out here. Hana, nine kilometres back, has a small station of limited hours, and the sensible riders carry enough to reach Kula or return to Paia without worry.

Come in the morning if you want the pull-off to yourself, or in a fresh wet spell when the falls are at their loudest. Swimming below the falls is possible for some people but the path is steep and slippery, and rocks fall and flash floods happen, so be careful and read any signs. Bikes should be parked well out of the traffic lane. Because the road here is narrow and visibility short, step across with attention, and keep your helmet and gear close. Then go on south, with the road running dry and wide-skied beyond Kipahulu.
t.kipahulu@20.7,-156.0:
Past Hana the traffic thins out, the road gets patchier, and you finally reach the part of Maui that tourists skip because they have run out of daylight. Kīpahulu is the quiet far corner of Haleakalā National Park, a detached coastal unit where the crater's rain runs down in a series of terraced pools and falls to the sea at ʻOheʻo Gulch. The old guidebook name, the Seven Sacred Pools, was a hotel marketing invention rather than anything Hawaiian, and the rangers will happily tell you so. There are more than seven, and what you can swim in changes with the weather and the rules.

The ride in is the reward and also the warning. From Hana, the road continues along the coast for about twelve kilometres, through rainforest tunnels, past waterfalls that come and go, and over narrow bridges that make you slow down whether you want to or not. The pavement is rougher here, with frost-heaved patches and the occasional rockfall. The humidity is thick, the light is green, and the smell of wet ginger and mango hangs over everything. Take it gently, because the uphill side is blind and oncoming cars are often hired.

At the end, the National Park maintains a visitor area with a fee at the gate, toilets, and a trailhead. The Pīpīwai trail climbs through a bamboo forest, one of the more eerie places you can walk in the islands, to Waimoku Falls, a long, thin ribbon of water dropping a hundred metres or so. Carry rain gear and wear boots rather than motorcycle shoes if you plan to go all the way. Flash floods in the stream are real, and pools are closed when the water is high.

A little back along the coast is the Palapala Hoʻomau Church, a whitewashed chapel where Charles Lindbergh is buried. He spent his last years here in a modest house after a life of aviation and controversy, and the grave is beside the church above the sea. It is easy to miss and worth the detour.

Hana has the nearest pump, and its hours are short, so fill up in Pāʻia or Kahului before you commit. Turn around with a full tank and enough light, and treat this as the end of the world, which on this island it more or less is.
t.soloneshnoye@51.7,84.3:
Soloneshnoye is a village of about five thousand people in the foothills of the Altai, in Altai Krai, and it is the kind of place that most travellers see only from a car window on the way to something more famous. The land here is a transition: to the north and west stretches the Ob steppe, a wide plain of wheat fields and shelterbelts, and to the south and east the ground begins to rise into wooded hills, the first low ridges of the Altai Mountains. The soil is rich and dark, the villages are wooden and neat, and in July the fields shimmer with sunflowers and ripening grain.

This part of Siberia was settled by Russian peasants in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and the region has a history of silver mining and smelting that goes back to the Demidov family, whose works in the Altai supplied the imperial mint. The Old Believers, who fled religious persecution, also settled the valleys, and their descendants still keep distinctive customs in some villages. Today the economy is mostly farming, with dairy, grain and beekeeping, and Altai honey, with its clear, aromatic taste, is sold at roadside stalls and in village shops.

The riding here is gentle and unhurried. The roads run through rolling farmland and birch groves, with long, easy bends, and the surface is generally decent, though patched, with frost heave and occasional potholes. Traffic is light, mainly farm vehicles and local cars, and the scenery changes slowly from fields to forest as you head toward the mountains. In summer, the weather is warm, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and in autumn, the birches turn gold. Winters are long and cold, with deep snow, and the roads can be icy. The best months are June to September.

Practical matters are simple. Larger supplies are available in the bigger towns on the main road, and for accommodation, the choices are limited, with guest houses and the occasional small hotel. Fill up before heading into the hills, where stations become less frequent.

If you want a taste of the countryside before the mountains, stop at a roadside stall and buy a jar of honey. The shop assistant will probably tell you which valley the bees visited.
t.denisova cave@51.4,84.7:
Few caves on earth have earned a place in the textbooks the way this one has. Denisova Cave sits on a limestone slope above the Anuy River in the northwestern Altai, and the story goes that it took its name from a hermit called Dionisy, Denis in the local speech, who lived here in the eighteenth century. What matters now is what lay in the floor. In 2010 a tiny finger bone from these deposits turned out to belong to a human group nobody had known about, the Denisovans, and later work showed that Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern people all passed through this same chamber at different times. You are standing where three kinds of humanity took shelter from the same winters.

Getting here is half the point. From Belokurikha you work west and north through the foothill farmland towards Soloneshnoye, the last proper town on the way with some four and a half thousand people, and that is where you should fill the tank and buy water, because the village of Topolnoye further on is small and the final miles are rural road and track. Expect a mix of tired asphalt and gravel, the odd cattle crossing, and a surface that turns greasy after rain. A light bike with sensible tyres is happier here than a loaded tourer, and the mood is of a valley that sees few visitors outside summer.

The Anuy valley itself is gentle country of birch, pine and meadow rather than the dramatic peaks you meet further south in the Altai, with the river running clear over stones and the slopes holding the grass smell of a dry continental summer. Late spring and early autumn are kind, the first with fresh green and the second with gold in the birches. July can be hot, and the cave mouth, cool and a little damp, makes a welcome shade.

Plan your visit with a bit of humility. This is still a working scientific site, so access to the interior depends on the day and the guides, and it is worth asking in Belokurikha or Soloneshnoye about the current arrangements before you ride the last stretch. Even if the gates are shut, the view from the slope, with the river curling below and the same horizon the cave dwellers had, makes the detour worth it. Bring a layer for the shade, eat before you come, and give yourself time to sit and look at a very old doorstep.
t.waimea canyon lookout@22.1,-159.7:
Waimea Canyon is often called the Grand Canyon of the Pacific, and when you step up to the lookout, the comparison is not absurd. The canyon is some ten miles long and a mile wide, and it drops more than three thousand feet, a trench of red, orange and green cut into the west side of Kauai, with ridges and buttes rising from the floor and a thin ribbon of river far below. Waterfalls streak the walls after rain, and in the early morning the colours glow.

It is an unexpected sight in the middle of the Pacific. Kauai is a volcanic island, and the canyon was formed by a combination of volcanic collapse and the work of the Waimea River, which has been cutting into the lava layers for millions of years. The red comes from iron in the soil, and the green from forest and shrubs on the ledges. Waimea means reddish water in Hawaiian, a name that comes from the river's colour after rain, when mud washes down from the canyon walls. The canyon walls reveal layers of ancient lava flows like pages in a book.

The ride up Waimea Canyon Drive is excellent. The road climbs from the coast near Waimea town in a series of curves, through dry forest and red earth, with viewpoints along the way, rising to cooler air and fresh smells of eucalyptus and moist soil. The surface is paved but patched, with potholes in places, tight curves and blind corners, and tour vans and rental cars stopping suddenly for photographs. Mornings are best, before cloud builds and traffic thickens, and the lookout is much clearer before noon. Rain can come at any time, and the road can be slick, with fog on the upper sections.

Wildlife includes feral goats on the canyon walls, and sometimes rare native birds in the forest higher up. The weather up here is cooler than the beach, so bring a jacket, particularly if you plan to continue to the higher lookouts.

Waimea and Kekaha on the coast, about twelve kilometres below, have petrol stations, shops and restaurants, so fill the tank before you climb. There are toilets at the lookout and sometimes a stand selling drinks, but little else.

Try to arrive early, stay long enough to see the light change, and keep an eye on the clouds, which can fill the canyon in minutes.
t.kalalau lookout@22.2,-159.7:
Kalalau Lookout is the place on Kauai where the road ends and the cliffs begin. From the railed platform, you look down into the Kalalau Valley, a deep green amphitheatre of fluted ridges that drops more than four thousand feet to the sea, with the surf of the Nā Pali coast glinting at the bottom. It is one of the most celebrated views in Hawaii, and when the weather cooperates, it is hard to turn away from.

The weather is the main thing to know. Clouds roll up from the ocean and pour into the valley, and a clear view can vanish in seconds, and return minutes later, so the usual advice is to wait. Many visitors arrive, see only white mist and leave, and miss the moment when the curtain lifts. The valley itself is remote and wild, long uninhabited, though Hawaiians once farmed taro there and the place holds old stone terraces. The cliffs are dense with ferns, native trees and falls that run down after rain, and the whole scene carries a feeling of age and isolation.

The road to the lookout, along Kōkeʻe Road past the canyon, rises through cooler forest of koa, ohia and eucalyptus, with the smell of damp earth and the sound of birds. It is a pleasant, winding ride on paved road, patched in places, with dips, blind curves and slow traffic, and rain makes it slippery. The air gets noticeably cooler as you climb, and mist is common in the afternoon, so go early. Feral chickens and sometimes goats wander the verges, and rare native birds, including the bright red iiwi, can be heard in the trees.

Kōkeʻe State Park, which surrounds the area, has trails and a small museum and lodge that sometimes sell food and drinks, though hours vary. Fuel and supplies are far below, in Waimea or Kekaha, around twenty kilometres from here, and Princeville on the north shore is similarly distant by road, so bring a full tank and some snacks. A warm jacket is useful.

Wait at the railing if the clouds are in. The view is worth the patience, and the silence when the mist parts is something you will remember.
t.waimea kauai@22.0,-159.7:
Waimea means reddish water in Hawaiian, and the name is earned: the river that gives the town its name carries a good deal of red soil down from the canyon after rain. It is a small, sleepy place on the dry western side of Kauai, strung out along the shore, with low houses, a few shops and cafes, and a surprisingly big place in history. In January 1778, Captain James Cook anchored off this coast, the first recorded European contact with the Hawaiian islands, and a statue in town commemorates the visit.

The other relic is Fort Elizabeth, a ruined stone fortress at the river mouth, built in 1817 by agents of a Russian trading company who hoped to gain a foothold in the islands. It was abandoned within a couple of years, but the walls of lava rock remain, and are now a state historic site. West Kauai in general feels slower and less polished than the north shore, and many of the local families have been here for generations.

The ride begins here, climbing out of the sunny coastal plain into the mountains on the road to Waimea Canyon. The road rises quickly, through scrubby red hills and eucalyptus, with several tight bends and some steep sections, and views open to the ocean and the island of Niihau on the horizon. Before long the canyon appears: an enormous gorge of red, green and brown, carved by the river and the weather, often called the Grand Canyon of the Pacific. It is not quite as large as the original, but its colours are glorious, especially when the clouds break.

Fuel and food are here, or in nearby Kekaha, so make sure the tank is full, because the upper roads have none. Lihue, over thirty kilometres away, is the main town on the island. West-side weather is usually sunny at the shore, and cloud and drizzle can sit over the canyon, so take a jacket. Early morning is best, with the clearest views and the least traffic, since the tour vans come later in the day. Afterwards, try a plate lunch, a local mix of rice, macaroni salad and grilled meat or fish, from one of the small stands.
t.puu o kila@22.2,-159.7:
The road finishes in a car park at a lookout, and the lookout finishes in a cliff. Puʻu o Kila sits at the high end of Kōkeʻe State Park on Kauai, at about four thousand feet, and from the railing the land drops away in one great fold into Kalalau Valley, a steep green amphitheatre of ridges and fluted walls that runs out to the Pacific and the Nā Pali coast. Even on a clear morning, a white cloud can slide in and fill the valley in minutes, then clear again just as quickly, so patience is part of the stop.

Kalalau was once home to a community of Hawaiian farmers who grew taro in terraces on the valley floor and fished from the shore. Now it is empty, protected, and accessible only by a long coastal trail or by boat. The lookout is the only easy way to see it, and the shapes of the ridges, the waterfalls after heavy rain, and the sound of birds in the forest give the place a deep sense of remoteness. Native forest birds, including the bright red iiwi, live up here, in ʻōhiʻa trees.

The ride up is the great part. Starting at Waimea, the road goes along the rim of the canyon, with a series of lookouts, and then continues into the cool forest of Kōkeʻe. The surface is paved and in decent condition, with long climbs and tight curves, and traffic is often heavy with tour vans from late morning. Mist and rain are possible at any time, because these ridges are among the wettest places on Earth, and the temperature can be ten degrees cooler than at the coast. Wear a rain jacket and bring a warm layer.

Kekaha is about twenty kilometres back down the hill. A small lodge and a cafe near the park headquarters offer snacks and a hot drink, but opening times vary, so do not rely on them. The best time is early, when the sky is likely to be clear, and the winter months bring more rain and mud on the trails. Take care not to leave the road, as the cliffs are unfenced in places and the ground is crumbly.
t.waimea@20.0,-155.7:
Waimea is cowboy country, and that is a strange thing to find on a tropical island. The town, also known by its postal name Kamuela, lies on a high, cool, windy plateau at about twenty-five hundred feet, between the Kohala Mountains and the huge bulk of Mauna Kea. The land is open grass, dotted with eucalyptus windbreaks, cattle and horses, and on a misty morning it looks a lot more like Scotland or Wyoming than Hawaii.

The ranching tradition goes back to the early nineteenth century, when cattle were brought to the island and ran wild until Mexican and Spanish vaqueros were brought over to teach the Hawaiians how to handle them. The Hawaiian cowboys became known as paniolo, a word derived from español, and their saddles, ropes and slack-key guitar music are all part of the heritage. The Parker Ranch, founded in the 1840s by a sailor named John Palmer Parker, grew into one of the largest ranches in the United States. Waimea has a cattle culture that you can taste in the local beef.

For a rider arriving from Hilo on the Saddle Road, the town is a good reward. After a long traverse through lava fields and cloud, you drop into green pastures, the air warms up and smells of grass, and the first stores appear. The road is paved and the bends are long, so the ride is easy, but the wind can be strong, and rain showers come in from the east without much notice. Take care in the evening, when mist can reduce visibility, and watch for cattle and wild pigs on rural roads.

Waimea is the main town on this side of the island, with about nine thousand people, which means it has everything you need, including fuel stations, supermarkets, cafes and restaurants. Fill up here, because there is little else for long stretches in either direction. Farmers' markets on weekends sell vegetables, flowers and Big Island coffee, and it is a good place to try a plate of local beef. From here, the road continues down to the sunny, dry Kohala coast, a world away, with beaches and resorts, only twenty minutes down the hill.
t.near hana@20.7,-156.0:
By the time you reach the Hana end of the Hana Highway, you have earned it. The road from Kahului winds along the north-east coast of Maui for about eighty kilometres, with hundreds of bends and dozens of narrow bridges, most of them only one lane wide, through rainforest, past waterfalls and above black lava cliffs. Hana itself is a small, quiet town of about twelve hundred people, set around a bay with a red cinder hill, Ka'uiki, guarding its southern end.

The country beyond Hana is some of the loveliest in Hawaii. Hamoa Beach, a crescent of grey sand under palms, was singled out by the writer James Michener as one of the most beautiful beaches in the Pacific. North of town, Wai'anapanapa State Park has a black sand beach, sea caves and lava arches, and it now requires advance reservations. South, the road continues to Kipahulu, part of Haleakala National Park, where the Pools of 'Ohe'o tumble down to the sea, and a little further on, in the churchyard of a small stone church, the aviator Charles Lindbergh is buried. He spent his last years in the area and chose to be buried looking out to sea.

The riding is slow and beautiful. The road is narrow, with tight bends and blind corners, and it is busy with tourists in rental cars who stop suddenly to look at waterfalls. At the one-lane bridges, the custom is to let groups of cars cross in turn, and patience is essential. Rain is frequent, especially in the morning, and the road can be slippery with mud, leaves and water. Beyond Kipahulu, the road becomes rougher, and many rental agreements do not allow you to continue around the back of Haleakala.

Hana has a small fuel station, a few shops, food trucks and a hotel, but services are limited, and fuel is expensive. Kula, about thirty-three kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, is the nearest larger community. Fill up in Paia or Kahului before you set out, and bring water and snacks.

Remember that people live here, and the road is their only link to the rest of the island. Drive with courtesy, park only in designated areas and respect private land.
